overview: The Transvaal record crosses several governments: British annexation, the restored South African Republic, war, and a British colony. Gold mining transformed the region, drawing workers and investors into a society in which white political rights coexisted with coercive controls over African residents.

periods.title: British annexation
periods.summary: British rule began with annexation in 1877 and ended after the first Anglo-Boer war.

periods.title: Restored republic
periods.summary: Republican government returned in 1881; the war of 1899 to 1902 ended its independence.

periods.title: Colony, then Union
periods.summary: British colonial government was followed by incorporation into the Union in 1910.

items.text: The map begins in 1878, just after Britain annexed the South African Republic in 1877. Republican government returned in 1881 after war. These changes matter: “Transvaal” names a region whose government and relationship with Britain changed during the same map interval.

Gold discovered on the Witwatersrand in 1886 brought prospectors, industrialists and work-seekers from far beyond the region. Mines and the growing city of Johannesburg transformed the landscape. Their wealth depended on labour as well as geology, and left lasting environmental damage.

Industrial development included much more than extracting gold. Sammy Marks and partners built a distillery at Eerste Fabrieken, followed by glass and jam or preserve factories. Bottles and preserved food linked manufacturing to things people used in everyday households.

Mine dust could cause silicosis, a serious lung disease. Elaine Katz’s research on the mines from 1886 to 1910 shows how owners promoted the unsupported idea that short contracts protected African workers. A worker returning home could still carry the consequences of dangerous work.

The Pioneer Museum preserves an 1848 farmhouse at Hartebeestpoort with clay walls, a thatched roof and earthen floors. Its present furnishings interpret nineteenth-century rural life. Local building materials produced a very different home from the later grand houses of mining wealth.

That museum surrounds the house with a traditional herb and vegetable garden, orchard, vineyard and wagon house. These are interpreted surroundings, not an untouched 1848 garden. They help visitors think of a farm home as a workplace that grew food and maintained transport.

At Zwartkoppies, the Marks family’s later house grew to forty rooms. Sammy and Bertha had first lived in a simple thatched clay house while the new home was built. Their move makes the contrast between modest shelter and concentrated industrial wealth unusually tangible.

The Sammy Marks Museum reports that almost all its displayed household contents belonged to the family, including silver, porcelain and furniture. Unlike a room assembled from unrelated period pieces, this collection can reveal one affluent household’s choices. It remains one family’s life, not everybody’s.

Paul and Gezina Kruger’s Pretoria home was built in 1884 and is now furnished to reflect their residence. The museum also preserves the president’s railway coach. House and carriage show how political office connected a domestic household to official travel.

Beside Kruger’s house, the site remembered as gaMohle was associated with enforcing pass laws from 1896. The standing commissioner’s building dates from 1932. Its earlier history exposes the restrictions imposed on African movement alongside the republic’s claims to freedom from Britain.

sections.title: Print and the end of the republic

items.text: “De Volksstem” is a short Dutch writing sample from the title of a Pretoria newspaper first issued in 1873. It means “The People’s Voice”. The University of Pretoria preserves historical documentation of the paper; the familiar-looking Latin letters carried Dutch, rather than automatically Afrikaans.

The war of 1899 to 1902 extended far beyond armies. African people worked as scouts, drivers, blacksmiths and builders, and British forces confined both Boer families and Black civilians in camps. Food shortages, poor sanitation and disease made civilian life perilous.

ending.text: The Treaty of Vereeniging on 31 May 1902 ended the republic’s independence. The Transvaal subsequently became a province of the Union of South Africa in 1910. Farmers, miners, towns and African communities continued through these political transformations; the imported 1914 endpoint is not a separate fall.
